targets.why_hot: A read-only walk of a 12,000-field operation allocates 23,749 object blocks and returns the original document. visit still builds a fresh 5-tuple, (in_array, idx, keys, edits, stack), for every AST node when the visitor has no enter or leave method and edits stays None. Reusing one frame buffer would keep that document identity and the same enter/leave order while dropping those tuples.

targets.why_hot: Lexing a 2,500-line indented block string peaks at 493,112 traced bytes, several times the dedented token value. The scanner grows each raw line with +=, dedent_block_string_lines slices every indented line into a second string, and join builds the token while both copies are live. The token value is the spec BlockStringValue. One dedenting buffer would keep that string and lower the peak.

targets.why_hot: A flat list of 50,000 ints under [Int] returns False and peaks at 3,516,880 traced bytes. Before any element is popped, the depth check extends its stack with one (value, type, depth) tuple per element, so the whole width is live at once. The only observable result is that bool. An index walk would return the same bool without the tuple stack.

targets.why_hot: Completing a sync list of 6,000 ints allocates 41,760 object blocks, about 7 per item, and the response list equals the input. Each item builds a Path via add_key (about 2 of those blocks, including the index integer) and then calls complete_list_item_value, complete_value, and complete_leaf_value. The returned ints do not depend on those Path objects. Completing successful leaf items without a per-item Path would keep the list and the error paths for items that fail.
